body:
# Independent audit and intrinsic extension of whole-fiber capture

Audited `candidate a222e8a47d0c28ff`.
Result: the original full mixed-volume theorem and its separately
stated n=0 and d=0 cases pass independent audit. The intrinsic extension
proved below has since been incorporated into the theorem file at the
parent's request, after the parent independently checked its dimension
argument. In particular, the hypothesis only requires
that SOME original cap fully capture each positive fiber; other caps
may slice that same fiber.

The proof correctly uses positive STRICTLY negative remainders, so a
vertical closed cap retains an entire boundary fiber. The sets of
uncaptured bases are lattice-convex even when the captured fractions
are not zero-or-one. Their individual nonempty remainders are not
mistaken for a common remainder in a single fiber. Empty convex hulls
are harmless, and the original caps, rather than replacements, survive
the Doignon extraction. The binary product example proves both stated
sharpness assertions exactly.

## Direct extension to the task's intrinsic measure

In fact this particular theorem extends directly to intrinsic H_q.
No thickening or limiting argument is needed.

Let C be compact and convex, let S=C intersect (Z^n x R^d) be nonempty,
and write K_z=C_z for its finitely many nonempty fibers. Put

    q=max_z dim_aff K_z,
    P={z:dim_aff K_z=q},
    w_z=H_q(K_z) for z in P,
    M=sum_(z in P) w_z.

The Hausdorff dimension of S is q, and its H_q mass is this sum:
each fiber is an isometric copy of K_z, different fibers are disjoint,
and lower-dimensional convex fibers have zero H_q measure when q>0.
For q=0 every nonempty fiber is a singleton, H_0 counts it, and P is
the set of all nonempty fiber bases. Thus 0<M<infinity in all cases.

Suppose a finite family of closed ambient caps has the property that
for each z in P some cap captures H_q-almost all of K_z. Then at most
2^n of those ORIGINAL caps still have this property, and some original
cap has H_q mass at least M/2^n.

Here is the only additional geometric verification needed. If an
integer w is a convex combination sum t_l z_l of points of P, discard
zero coefficients. Convexity gives

    sum_l t_l K_(z_l) subset K_w.

The left-hand side has affine dimension at least q: fix points in all
but one summand and retain a scaled q-dimensional body in that one.
The right-hand side has dimension at most q by its definition as the
maximum dimension of ALL integer fibers. Therefore K_w has dimension
exactly q, so w belongs to P. This proves conv(P) intersect Z^n=P.

For a cap H={a.z+u.x>=b}, set

    Q_H={z in P:H_q(K_z minus H_z)>0}.

For every z_l in Q_H, the strictly negative portion contains a
nonempty relatively open q-dimensional ball E_l in aff K_(z_l).
For q>0 this follows from positive measure and the nullity of the
relative boundary of a q-dimensional convex body. For q=0 take its
single strictly negative point. If w=sum t_l z_l is integer, the
Minkowski combination sum t_l E_l lies strictly outside H_w by
affinity and is contained in K_w. It contains a relatively open
q-dimensional ball: again, fix points in all but one positive-weight
summand. Since K_w has dimension exactly q, this ball has positive
H_q measure in K_w. Thus w belongs to Q_H.

This proves conv(Q_H) intersect Z^n=Q_H. No common fiber-direction
space was assumed. If varying directions could make the Minkowski
sum have larger dimension, its inclusion in the integer fiber K_w
would contradict maximality of q; the dimension argument already
rules out that possibility at every representation used here.

The rest of the original Doignon argument is unchanged. The full
capture hypothesis says intersection_H Q_H is empty. The convex sets
conv(Q_H) therefore have integer-free intersection; choose at most
2^n by Doignon. Every positive-q-volume fiber is captured almost
entirely by one selected original cap. Summing their H_q masses gives
M<=sum_selected H_q(S intersect H)<=2^n max_H H_q(S intersect H).

All comparisons use the task's fixed intrinsic H_q, with its usual
normalization. No affine change of variables, omitted boundary mass,
or conversion to ambient volume occurs. For n=0, full capture of the
single fiber immediately gives the one-cap conclusion instead of
requiring a formulation of Doignon in dimension zero.

The extension still requires whole-fiber capture. It gives no bound
for a cover whose traces are genuinely partial on every cap at one
of the positive fibers, and therefore does not establish OC.
note: Mathematical discussion retained to expose corrections and limitations. This is not a verification run, accepted premise, or approval of the revised submission. Association follows explicit source-document references, not an inferred dependency.
